title: soft-affinity-heuristics-preemptive-scheduler-notes
content:
Context and motivation:

We keep seeing short-lived requests (small prompt, short generate) with high variability in tail latency even on otherwise idle nodes. Flamegraphs point at sporadic thread parking/unparking, syscall wakes, and Python GIL holds during request preproc/parse. Previous notes focused on tokenizer micro-optimizations and fast-pathing parsing; this doc explores a complementary approach: soft-affinity + lightweight preemptive scheduling heuristics to reduce wake-up jitter and GIL handoff cost for tiny requests.

Goals:
- Reduce 95/99 latency for <50-token requests by 15–30% without impacting throughput for heavy batches.
- Avoid radical runtime changes (no full rewrite of request pipeline).
- Keep heuristics tunable per workload/customer.

Hypotheses (quick):
1) Aggressive strict CPU-affinity increases cache locality but causes cold wakes when a request is scheduled on a remote core (cross-socket wake -> pipeline stalls).
2) Allowing soft affinity (preferred core but permit steal) plus a short preemption window reduces queueing spikes from long-lived tasks.
3) Introducing a bounded preemptive yield in the Python shim around blocking syscalls/tokenization can lower GIL-handover stalls for tiny requests.

Experimental setup (environment):
- Node: c6i.8xlarge (32 vCPU) equivalent internal lab machines (linux-6.x, jemalloc-5.3, python-3.11-pgo).
- Serving runtime: branch soft-affinity-experiments (PR 2387).
- Load generator: serving-load-gen v0.9; scenarios: small-echo (10–30 tokens), mixed (25% small, 75% 512-token).
- Collector: async perf-sampler + eBPF stackcounts (1s buckets) + occasional full perf script captures for pprof/flamegraph.

Key implementation notes:
- Soft affinity: worker threads have an ordered preference list (local logical core, buddy core, local socket pool, global pool). Threads will attempt to bind to preference list but are allowed to run anywhere if queue depth exceeds N (configurable).
- Preemptive window: tasks longer than X ms (configurable; default 5ms) are marked as preemptible. A lightweight scheduler thread uses tick-based cooperative checks and a SIGVTALRM fallback to nudge long-blocking native calls.
- Python shim change: add short periodical PyGILState_Unlock around known blocking parse/tokenize C-extensions and around I/O boundaries; implement best-effort tokenization fast-path that avoids acquiring GIL for pure-bytes operations (when extension returns pre-tokenized buffer).

Microbenchmarks and results (small-echo scenario):
Baseline (strict-affinity + no-preempt):
- p50: 3.2ms, p95: 18.6ms, p99: 52.3ms, QPS: 950
Soft-affinity + cooperative-preempt (no SIG nudge):
- p50: 3.0ms, p95: 14.2ms, p99: 41.7ms, QPS: 940
Soft-affinity + preemptive nudge (SIGVTALRM heuristic enabled):
- p50: 3.0ms, p95: 12.1ms, p99: 30.4ms, QPS: 930
Notes: absolute QPS drop is small (2–3%) in these builds; tail latency improvement is the main win. The SIGVTALRM path helped in cases where C-extensions block the interpreter for several ms.

Profile observations:
- eBPF stackcounts show reduced time in futex/wake paths when soft-affinity is enabled (less cross-core waking).
- perf flamegraphs show fewer long stacks where the Python thread is idle waiting on another thread to release GIL after tokenization.
- Occasional regressions: increased context-switch syscall counts when preemption window is too small (<3ms) due to over-eager yielding.

Edge cases and anomalies:
- Some third-party tokenizers (Rust/Python FFI) crash on SIG-based preemption if they don't set SA_RESTART properly; we added a whitelist for nudge-safe code paths.
- On NUMA boxes with strict memory placement, soft-affinity allowing cross-socket execution increased remote memory access for large-batch workloads; heuristic must bias toward socket-local for >N tokens.

Tuning knobs (configurable per node or per route):
- affinity_preference_depth (how many levels in preference list)
- preemptible_ms_threshold (default 5ms)
- nudge_backoff_ms (how frequently SIG nudge allowed per thread)
- socket_bias_token_threshold (switch to socket-local hard affinity for >X tokens)

Quick pseudocode for worker selection (simplified):

for incoming_request in accept_queue:
    pref_list = compute_pref_list(current_thread, request.meta)
    chosen = try_pop_worker_from(pref_list, steal_allowed=True)
    if not chosen and queue_depth > threshold:
        chosen = steal_from_global_pool()
    schedule_on(chosen)

Preemptive-nudge loop (driver thread):
    every 1ms:
        for thread in running_threads:
            if thread.run_ns > preemptible_ms_threshold * 1e6 and thread.safe_to_nudge:
                send_nudge(thread)  // SIGVTALRM or runtime API

Safety and correctness considerations:
- Debugging mode disables SIG nudges to assist reproducing crashes.
- Maintain a per-thread epoch counter so stale nudge signals for already-finished tasks are ignored.
- Instrumentation trace points for: affinity resolution, preemptible decision, nudge delivered, nudge handled, nudge ignored.

Operational experiments ran for 48 hours under mixed traffic. Observations:
- For PLG-style onboarding traffic (many tiny requests from single-tenant tests), p99 improved by ~35% on average for affected routes.
- For sustained high-batch workloads, throughput unchanged if socket_bias_token_threshold is tuned; otherwise soft-affinity can slightly decrease throughput due to remote memory latency.
- Memory usage pattern unchanged; no increase in resident set attributable to changes.

Compatibility checklist (before rolling to Dedicated):
- Ensure FFI/3rd-party C extensions used in tokenizers are registered as nudge-safe or tested with test harness that injects signals.
- Add e2e job in CI that exercises preemptive path under heavy fuzzed inputs.
- Add route-level config in console to toggle heuristics and per-tenant thresholds.

Next steps and experiments to run:
1) Replace SIGVTALRM path with a faster runtime-integrated checkpoint (avoid signal semantics) — prototype in rust-shim branch.
2) Add a lightweight kernel-batched wake optimization: group worker wake-ups for adjacent cores to reduce interrupt storms.
3) Expand microbench matrix: vary token lengths, open connections per second, and cold start vs. warm cache to quantify where heuristics break.
4) Run 7-day baseline vs. heuristics experiment on Dedicated nodes for two customers (low-latency chat vs. high-throughput embeddings) with feature-flagged rollout.

Open questions / unresolved:
- Best default for preemptible_ms_threshold across cloud types? (observed 4–6ms sweet spot on our lab machines)
- How to surface per-route recommendations in Console Optimize UI without overwhelming users with knobs?
- Will kernel-level wake coalescing help more than user-level soft-affinity in noisy multi-tenant shared infrastructure?

Appendix: commands and quick reproduce notes:
- start runtime with flags: --affinity-mode=soft --preemptible-ms=5 --nudge-enabled
- loadgen commands: ./serving-load-gen --scenario small-echo --concurrency 1000 --duration 1200
- perf collection: sudo perf record -F 99 -g --pid <runtime_pid> -- sleep 30; sudo perf script | flamegraph.pl > out.svg

Notes to self (short todo):
- add more fine-grained metrics for nudge rate per-core (grafana panel)
- create smoke test that toggles socket_bias_token_threshold and verifies no >2% throughput regression for batch workloads
- share results with SRE to validate kernel tunables (futex wake granularity)

References and related artifacts:
- PR: github.com/redwood-inference/serving-runtime/pull/2387 (soft-affinity prototype)
- Jira: RT-4123 preemptive-nudge-investigation
- Slack thread: #serving-runtime "soft-affinity experiments"

End of notes.
